name: store
description: Two ways to hand somebody a picture, and they are deliberately not the same thing. Publish it and it has a permanent public URL with no credential, no expiry and no audience. Or mint a grant: a code good for exactly one fetch and exactly N seconds, rendered as a QR code on the screen in front of the person you are showing it to. What the QR encodes is a PAGE about the code rather than the picture itself — it says the thing works once, counts the timer down, and carries the button that spends it — because everything that follows URLs without being the recipient (chat previews, prefetchers, scanners that open a link twice) used to burn the grant on the way. Now only a person pressing the button does; the raw bytes route still burns on fetch, which is what a script wants. The one-time part is a single conditional UPDATE that the database adjudicates rather than a read followed by a write, because two phones scanning the same code in the same instant is the ordinary case for a code on a screen. Time and use are independent bounds, so a code nobody ever scans is exactly as safe as one scanned once. Nothing here asks you to type a sha256: every place that names a picture takes the id, any unique prefix of it, the filename you stored it under, or `latest`, and two matches is an error naming both rather than a guess — the verbs behind it publish permanently and delete permanently. Durations are written the way people say them, 30s or 5m or 2h. Formats are decided by sniffing magic bytes and never by the filename, SVG is refused outright because it is a document that can carry script and this is served from an origin the whole fleet shares, and every image goes out under a content security policy that permits nothing. Storage is content-addressed with one row per owner, so the same picture held by two people costs the disk one copy. The console has the same store in four linkable screens and a DOCS tab rendered from the API's own /docs, which also answers a browser with a readable page and a program with JSON off the one dictionary. An agent gets eighteen MCP tools, two prompts and its pictures as resources over JSON-RPC on the API port — batched requests, event-stream replies, and real image content blocks back from view, qr and claim, because a claim answers after the code is already spent and that response is the only copy anyone gets. Peek and claim are kept as separate tools because a flag would have a default and a wrong default there cannot be undone.
route_note: unrouted by default. The public read path has no credential on it at all, so publishing this to the gateway publishes every image anyone on the box has published. Turn it on deliberately, not by inheriting a default.
backend: src/api/api.py (stdlib http.server — no framework, and the same src/ the CLI imports, so the console cannot drift from the command line). It also serves the share pages, /docs and the MCP endpoint: no second port for the agent, because this one already listens and already knows who is calling.
frontend: src/app/index.html served by src/app/server.py (stdlib) — the console at /store on :50671 in four screens (library, codes, published, docs+MCP), each addressable as a URL fragment so a reload keeps your place. It proxies /store/_api, /store/docs, /store/g/, /store/i/, /store/qr and /store/mcp so a share link is one origin. src/app/view.html is the page a scan lands on, served locally at /store/v/<code> and /store/p/<id> so it still renders while the API restarts.
state: ~/.mod/store-share — store.db (sqlite: the images and grants tables) and blobs/ (content-addressed image bytes, sharded two levels)
state_note: deliberately NOT ~/.mod/store, which is core/store's live database. See name_collision below.

name_collision.what: orbit/store is unreachable as a module. m.mod('store') resolves to core/store and always will.
name_collision.why: module names are derived from the directory path, and core/tree applies the orbits in an order that lets core overwrite orbit. The name field in this file is decorative for resolution.
name_collision.so: this works as an HTTP product on its own ports, and through `python3 mod.py <fn>` directly — the way orbit/chain does. It is not callable as `m store/fn`.
name_collision.if_you_want_it_callable: rename the directory. The previous occupant of this path hit the same wall and became orbit/shelf.
name_collision.unrelated_to: core/store, which is a general content-addressed store with its own tickets feature. This module is only about images.

identity.scheme: the fleet's shared protocol auth — m.mod('auth'), EIP-191 over secp256k1. The recovered address owns what it uploads.
identity.anonymous: over loopback only, an unauthenticated caller is the local owner from ~/.mod/store-share/owner.json, so the CLI and a browser on the box need not sign anything
identity.why_conditioned_on_the_bind: that shortcut is a full takeover if the port is ever reachable, so it keys off the interface actually bound rather than a config flag somebody flips without reading the note

sharing.publish: GET /i/<id> — permanent, uncredentialed, cacheable. As public as it sounds.
sharing.publish_page: GET /p/<id> — the same picture with a sentence about what the link is
sharing.grant: GET /g/<code> — one fetch, N seconds. Serving it burns it.
sharing.grant_page: GET /v/<code> — what the QR encodes. Opening it claims NOTHING; the button on it does.
sharing.why_a_page: a scan should land somewhere that says the thing works once and how long it has left, and an automated fetch — a link preview, a prefetch — should not be able to spend a grant meant for the person holding the phone
sharing.qr: GET /g/<code>/qr renders the page link, and never claims it — otherwise showing someone the code would spend it before they scanned it
sharing.revoke: DELETE /grant?code= kills a live code early; the screen showing it walked out of the room
sharing.max_ttl_note: a day is the ceiling because anything longer is publishing with extra steps, and publish is right there

one_time_guarantee.mechanism: UPDATE grants SET claimed=? WHERE code=? AND claimed IS NULL AND expires > ? — rowcount decides the winner
one_time_guarantee.why_not_read_then_write: two phones scanning the same on-screen code in the same instant is the ordinary case, and a check followed by a write hands the image to both
one_time_guarantee.diagnosis_is_advisory: the SELECT that turns a refusal into 'expired' or 'already used' runs after the UPDATE has already failed, and never authorises a claim
one_time_guarantee.spent_codes_are_kept: a deleted code is indistinguishable from one that never existed, so a burned link answers 410 rather than 404 and the holder can tell 'someone beat you to it' from 'you typed it wrong'

safety.formats: png, jpeg, gif, webp, bmp — decided by magic bytes, not by filename or claimed Content-Type
safety.svg: refused. Every other image format is inert data; SVG is a document that can carry script, and an origin shared with the whole fleet makes an uploaded SVG a stored-XSS primitive against the neighbours.
safety.headers: every image response carries Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; sandbox, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and an inline disposition — the second line for the day the first check is wrong
safety.grant_responses: no-store, so nothing between here and the phone keeps a copy of something that was good for one fetch
safety.private_probing: an unpublished id and an id that never existed both answer 404, so the public read path cannot be used to test whether a picture exists
safety.get_burns_the_grant: a QR scanner does a GET, so the claim must be a GET — but what the QR carries is the page, and the page claims nothing, so a chat preview, a prefetch or a HEAD all leave the code live and only a person pressing the button spends it. What remains is that the code is a credential in a URL and anyone the link reaches can press that button, which is why the default TTL is a minute: mint it when the person is in front of you.

optional.segno: pure-python QR encoder. Without it the links still work and only the pictures of them go missing.
optional.pillow: read image dimensions for the listing. Without it width and height are null.

env.STORE_SHARE_HOST: API bind (default 127.0.0.1 — read identity.py before changing)
env.STORE_SHARE_BASE: the origin share links are built from (default http://127.0.0.1:50671/store)
env.STORE_SHARE_SESSION_TTL: how long a signed token stays good (default 7d)
env.STORE_SHARE_MAX_INLINE: how large a picture may be before MCP hands back a URL instead of the bytes (default 1500000)

endpoints.docs: GET /docs?section=&format= — the manual: a readable page for a browser, JSON for anything that asks for JSON, off one dictionary
endpoints.my_bytes: GET /b/{id} — a picture you own, published or not. The one read path that checks who is asking.
endpoints.upload: POST /upload?name=&public= (raw image bytes as the body — no multipart)
endpoints.mcp: POST /mcp — JSON-RPC 2.0, one message or a batch
endpoints.mcp_schema: GET /mcp/schema — tools, prompts, resource templates and a client config

tests: tests/test_store.py — python3 -m pytest tests/ (84 passing; state is redirected to a tmpdir, nothing touches the real ~/.mod)

mcp.what: eighteen tools onto the same src/ the console and the CLI use — store_info, store_docs, store_health, store_images, store_public, store_image, store_view, store_add, store_share, store_publish, store_unpublish, store_grant, store_qr, store_grants, store_peek, store_claim, store_revoke, store_delete

transports.http: POST /mcp on the API port (or /store/mcp through the console)

mcp.batching: a JSON-RPC array is answered with an array of the replies that carry ids; a batch of nothing but notifications gets 202 and no body
mcp.streamable_http: a client accepting only text/event-stream gets one event and the stream ends — nothing here streams, and an idle open socket would only pretend otherwise
mcp.sessions: Mcp-Session-Id is echoed, not enforced: identity is already on every request in the Authorization header, so there is no session state to key. DELETE /mcp answers 204 so a clean disconnect is not logged as a failure.
mcp.pictures_come_back_as_pictures: store_view, store_qr and store_claim return image content blocks rather than a sentence about an image. claim especially: the code is spent by the time it answers, so that response is the only copy anyone gets.
mcp.resources: store://docs, store://docs/<section>, and store://image/<id> for each picture the caller owns — the nouns, for a client that lets a person attach context by hand
mcp.prompts: share_with_one_person names store_share and forbids store_publish; publish_forever makes the model look at the picture first. Two, because there are two ways to share and picking wrongly is the mistake this module exists to prevent.
mcp.no_second_port: the API already listens and already recovers the caller's address, so an agent over HTTP sees exactly what a browser with the same token would, and a remote caller with no token never reaches the tool layer
mcp.peek_is_not_claim: two tools rather than one tool with a flag: peek asks whether a code still works and spends nothing, claim redeems it and that IS spending it. A flag would have a default, and a wrong default there cannot be undone.

naming.what: no caller ever has to type a sha256
naming.a_picture: the full id, any unique prefix of it (4+ chars), the filename it was stored under, or `latest`
naming.ambiguity: an error naming every candidate, never a guess — the verbs behind the resolver publish permanently and delete permanently
naming.a_duration: 30s · 5m · 2h · 1d · or a bare number of seconds. ttl_seconds= still means seconds.
naming.a_code: the whole code. Prefixes resolve only for the owner who minted it and only off the public routes, because the code is the credential and a public prefix endpoint can be walked.
naming.where: src/resolve.py — one implementation, used by the CLI, the API and the MCP tools
